title: Video Production
description: Making a short video properly — pre-production (idea, script, storyboard, shot list), shots and angles, composition, recording good audio, editing and pacing, titles and credits, export formats, and copyright and permissions.

notes.heading: Pre-Production: Idea, Script, Storyboard, Shot List
notes.body: Video projects fail before filming starts or not at all: pre-production is where the quality is decided. Start with the idea — one clear message or story, a defined audience, and a realistic length (two minutes is plenty). Write the script next: what is said, by whom, and what is shown, in order. Even a factual video needs a script, because unscripted presenters ramble and repeat. Then storyboard the key shots: rough sketches of what the camera sees at each important moment, with notes on dialogue and timing. Finally, translate the storyboard into a shot list — the practical document used on the day: each shot numbered, its location, framing (wide or close), any movement, and the lines or action it covers. The shot list lets you film out of order (all shots in one location together, whatever their story order) and tick off coverage as you go. Also plan logistics now: who is in front of and behind the camera, what props and permissions are needed, and when and where you will film. Thirty minutes of planning saves hours of re-shooting.

notes.heading: Camera Shots and Angles
notes.body: Shot size is the vocabulary of visual storytelling. A wide (establishing) shot shows the whole scene and tells the audience where we are; a mid shot frames a person from the waist up and suits general action; a close-up fills the frame with a face or object and carries emotion or important detail; an extreme close-up isolates eyes or hands for intensity. Camera angle adds meaning: shooting from eye level feels neutral and honest; a low angle (camera looking up) makes the subject seem powerful or threatening; a high angle (looking down) makes them seem small or vulnerable; an over-the-shoulder shot looks past one person at another and is the standard way to film a conversation, keeping both people connected in the scene. A simple rule for interviews and dialogue: vary the shots. Record a wide shot of the whole exchange, then close-ups of each speaker, then cutaway shots (the interviewer nodding, the object being discussed) — these give you material to hide cuts and keep the edit visually alive. Random handheld wandering looks amateur; deliberate, held shots with a clear reason for each framing look professional.

notes.heading: Rule of Thirds and Composition
notes.body: Composition is how elements are arranged inside the frame. The rule of thirds is the foundational guide: imagine the frame divided by two horizontal and two vertical lines into nine equal boxes. Placing the subject on one of the lines — and key features like eyes at the intersections — produces a balanced, natural image, whereas dead-centre framing often feels static and dull. Supporting habits: give a person looking or moving sideways headroom and looking room (space in front of their face or direction of travel, not behind them); check the background for clutter and for the classic accident of a lamppost apparently growing out of someone's head; use natural frames like doorways and windows to draw the eye to the subject; and keep horizons level. In interviews, seat the subject so they look across the frame towards the interviewer beside the camera, with their eyes roughly on a thirds line. Rules can be broken deliberately for effect — centred symmetry can look powerful — but you should know the rule first so the break is a choice, not an accident. Review framing on the screen before pressing record, not after.

notes.heading: Recording Good Audio
notes.body: Audiences forgive shaky video; they will not sit through bad sound. Viewers rate a video's quality largely by its audio, so treat sound as a first-class job. The single biggest factor is microphone distance: a microphone close to the speaker (an arm's length or less) captures a clear voice and little room echo; the built-in microphone on a camera three metres away captures echo, wind and background noise. Choose the location for sound as much as for looks — quiet rooms with soft furnishings absorb echo, while empty halls and corridors boom; switch off fans and air conditioning, close windows, and warn others you are recording. Wind ruins outdoor audio, so shield the microphone or reposition. Always do a test recording and listen back with headphones before the real take, and monitor during recording if possible. Record a few seconds of the room's silence (room tone) to help smooth edits later, and clap or speak a label at the start of each take ('scene two, take three') so editing is faster. If a take has a phone ringing or a cough over a key line, re-record it immediately while everyone is still set up.

notes.heading: Editing: Cuts, Transitions, Pacing, Sound Levels
notes.body: Editing is where the film is actually made. Start by organising: import all clips, label them, and build a rough cut — the best takes in story order on the timeline, no polish yet. The basic edit is the cut: one shot instantly replaces another. Cuts are invisible when they follow the action — cutting on movement (as a hand reaches, as someone turns) feels natural — and jarring when they jump the subject's position mid-frame. Fancier transitions (dissolves, wipes, spins) should be rare and purposeful; a dissolve suggests time passing, and a star wipe mostly suggests you found the effects menu. Pacing is the rhythm of shot lengths: fast cutting builds energy, longer held shots create calm or tension, and most beginner videos are improved simply by trimming every shot to remove dead time at the start and end. Then balance the sound: dialogue loud and consistent across clips, music ducked well underneath speech, and effects timed to the picture. Finally, watch the whole thing with fresh eyes — or better, show someone else — and cut anything that does not serve the story. If a shot does not add information or feeling, it goes.

notes.heading: Titles, Credits and Export Formats
notes.body: Titles and credits frame the film professionally. An opening title names the video; lower thirds (text in the bottom third of the screen) identify speakers the first time they appear; closing credits list the team and, importantly, the sources of any music, images or clips used. Keep text legible: a simple sans-serif font, high contrast against the background (add a subtle shadow or bar behind text if the picture is busy), sized to read on a phone, and on screen long enough to read aloud twice. Check spelling — a misspelled name in the credits undermines the whole project. Exporting turns the editing project into a shareable file. The standard is MP4 using the H.264 codec: it plays on virtually every device and platform. Match the export to what you filmed — usually 1080p (1920×1080) at 25 or 30 frames per second — because exporting higher than the source adds size, not quality. File size depends on bitrate; most editors offer presets like 'high quality 1080p' that balance quality and size sensibly. Always watch the exported file from start to finish before sharing: export glitches, clipped endings and muted audio are only visible in the final file.

notes.heading: Copyright and Permissions for Media
notes.body: Everything in your video belongs to someone. Music, images, video clips, logos and sound effects are protected by copyright automatically — the creator does not have to register anything, and 'found it on the internet' is not a licence to use it. Using a commercial song as your soundtrack can get a video muted, blocked or removed when platforms detect it automatically. Safe sources: create it yourself; use copyright-free or Creative Commons libraries (checking the specific licence — some require credit, some forbid commercial use); or use assets bundled with your editing app. When a licence requires attribution, give it properly in the credits: track name, creator, source, licence. People need protecting too: filming someone is using their image, so get permission — ideally a simple written release for anything beyond classroom-only use — and take extra care with anyone younger. The same applies to private property, artwork and branded products in shot. 'Fair use' is a narrow legal concept, not a student project loophole; assuming everything needs permission until you have checked is the professional habit. Keep a list of every asset and its source as you build — scrambling to find them at credits time never works.

flashcards.definition: All the planning done before filming: idea, script, storyboard, shot list, locations, props and permissions.
flashcards.example: Thirty minutes writing a shot list saves hours of re-shooting missed angles.

flashcards.definition: A numbered checklist of every shot to film — framing, location, action — used on the day to track coverage.
flashcards.example: Shot 4: close-up of hands opening the box, kitchen, no dialogue.

flashcards.definition: A wide shot at the start of a scene showing the whole location so the audience knows where they are.
flashcards.example: A wide view of the school field before cutting to the close-up interview.

flashcards.definition: A shot framed past one person's shoulder towards another, the standard way to film conversations while keeping both people connected.
flashcards.example: An interview filmed past the interviewer's shoulder at the guest answering.

flashcards.definition: A composition guide dividing the frame into nine boxes; placing subjects on the lines or intersections gives balanced, natural images.
flashcards.example: Positioning an interviewee's eyes on the upper thirds line, looking across the empty two-thirds.

flashcards.definition: Empty space left in front of a person's face or direction of movement, rather than behind them, so the frame feels balanced.
flashcards.example: A runner framed on the left with open space to the right they are running into.

flashcards.definition: A shot of something related but separate from the main action, used to hide cuts and add visual variety.
flashcards.example: The interviewer nodding, or a close-up of the project being discussed, cut in over a trimmed answer.

flashcards.definition: A few seconds of recorded 'silence' from the filming location, used to smooth audio edits in post-production.
flashcards.example: Recording ten seconds of the empty room so a cut between takes does not change the background hiss abruptly.

flashcards.definition: The basic edit where one shot instantly replaces another; smoothest when made on movement.
flashcards.example: Cutting from a wide shot to a close-up as a hand reaches for a door handle feels invisible.

flashcards.definition: The rhythm of a film created by shot length and cutting speed — fast cuts for energy, longer holds for calm or tension.
flashcards.example: Trimming dead time at the start and end of every shot instantly tightens a beginner video.

flashcards.definition: A text caption in the bottom third of the screen identifying a speaker or place.
flashcards.example: "Amina — Robotics Club" appearing the first time Amina speaks.

flashcards.definition: The standard export format for sharing video — plays on virtually every device and platform with good quality at sensible file sizes.
flashcards.example: Exporting the finished film as a 1080p, 25 fps MP4 so anyone can play it.

questions.stem: Which document lists every shot to film — its framing, location and action — and is ticked off during the shoot?
choices: The credits
The shot list
The export preset
The lower third
questions.explanation: The shot list translates the storyboard into a practical filming checklist, letting you shoot out of story order (by location) while guaranteeing nothing is missed.

questions.stem: What is the main purpose of a wide (establishing) shot at the start of a scene?
choices: To show off the camera's zoom
To show the whole location so the audience knows where the scene is set
To hide the actors' faces
To test the microphone
questions.explanation: An establishing shot orients the viewer — the whole street, room or field — before closer shots focus on people and detail. Without it, audiences can feel lost about where they are.

questions.stem: Under the rule of thirds, where should a subject's eyes usually sit in an interview frame?
choices: Exactly in the centre of the frame
On or near an upper intersection of the thirds lines, with looking room in front of their face
At the very bottom edge
Anywhere — placement makes no difference
questions.explanation: Thirds-line placement with space in front of the face produces a balanced, natural frame. Dead-centre framing often feels static, and placing the face against the edge they look towards feels cramped.

questions.stem: What is the single biggest factor in recording clear spoken audio?
choices: Buying the most expensive camera
Getting the microphone close to the speaker — within about an arm's length
Recording in a large empty hall
Filming at the highest possible resolution
questions.explanation: Microphone distance dominates audio quality: close mics capture a clear voice with little echo, while distant built-in mics capture the room. A modest microphone near the speaker beats a great camera far away.

questions.stem: Why do editors prefer the plain cut over fancy transitions like spins and star wipes?
choices: Cuts use less computer memory
Cuts are invisible when timed with the action, while gimmicky transitions distract from the story
Fancy transitions are only available on expensive software
Cuts automatically fix bad lighting
questions.explanation: A cut placed on movement feels natural and keeps attention on content. Effects transitions announce themselves and pull viewers out of the story; dissolves survive because they meaningfully signal time passing.

questions.stem: Which export settings are the sensible standard for sharing a school video online?
choices: AVI at the largest possible bitrate
MP4 (H.264) at 1080p and the frame rate you filmed at
A sequence of individual JPEG images
The editing project file itself
questions.explanation: MP4 with the H.264 codec plays on almost every device. Matching resolution and frame rate to the source keeps quality without bloating file size; a project file only opens in the editing software.

questions.stem: A friend wants to use their favourite chart song as the soundtrack of a video to be posted online. What is the correct advice?
choices: Fine — short videos are exempt from copyright
Do not: commercial music is protected and platforms detect it automatically; use self-made, library, or properly licensed Creative Commons music instead
Fine if the song is credited in the description
Fine if the video is only shared with friends
questions.explanation: Copyright applies automatically and crediting does not grant a licence. Platforms automatically detect commercial music and mute or block the video. Safe choices are your own recordings, app libraries, or Creative Commons tracks used within their licence terms.

questions.stem: During editing, an answer in an interview needs a sentence removed from the middle, which creates a visible jump cut in the speaker's face. What is the standard professional fix?
choices: Leave the jump — audiences never notice
Cover the cut with a cutaway shot (the interviewer nodding, or a close-up of the subject discussed) while the trimmed audio continues
Re-shoot the entire interview in one perfect take
Blur the speaker's face at the cut point
questions.explanation: Cutaways exist precisely for this: the picture shows related material while the audio edit happens underneath, making the removal invisible. This is why shooting cutaways and noddies during the interview matters.

questions.stem: A scene needs to make a character look powerful and intimidating. Which camera choice supports that?
choices: A high angle looking down at them
A low angle looking up at them
A shaky handheld close-up of their feet
An overexposed wide shot
questions.explanation: Low angles make the subject loom over the viewer, reading as power or threat; high angles do the opposite, making subjects look small and vulnerable. Angle is a storytelling tool, not just a viewpoint.

questions.stem: Your filmed dialogue sounds hollow and echoey, with a fan humming throughout. Which combination of fixes actually solves it for the re-shoot?
choices: Turn up the microphone volume and add background music to hide it
Move to a smaller room with soft furnishings, switch the fan off, place the microphone close to the speaker, and listen back to a test recording first
Shout the lines so the voice drowns out the echo
Film at night when sound travels less
questions.explanation: Echo and background noise are location and placement problems: soft furnishings absorb reflections, removing noise sources beats covering them, close mics capture voice over room, and test recordings catch problems before the real take.

questions.stem: Why is it useful to film a conversation with a wide shot plus close-ups of each speaker, rather than one continuous wide shot?
choices: It uses up spare memory cards
It gives editing options — you can hide trims, emphasise reactions, and keep the scene visually varied
One wide shot is always better; this is a trick question
It makes the set look bigger than it is
questions.explanation: Multiple angles are editing raw material: cutting between shots lets you remove mistakes invisibly, show the listener's reaction at key moments, and prevent visual monotony. A single static wide offers none of these options.

questions.stem: Your finished two-minute video feels slow, though the content is good. What is the first editing change to try?
choices: Add spin transitions between every shot
Trim the dead time at the start and end of every shot so each cut lands on action
Re-film everything at a higher frame rate
Make the music louder throughout
questions.explanation: Most beginner pacing problems are dead time — seconds of nothing before and after the action in each shot. Tightening every shot to its useful content transforms the rhythm without any new footage or effects.

questions.stem: Which is the correct approach to filming a classmate for a video that will be shown outside the classroom?
choices: Film them secretly so the footage looks natural
Get their permission — ideally a simple written release — before filming, and respect a refusal
Film anyone; only celebrities have image rights
Get permission only from the teacher, never the person filmed
questions.explanation: A person's image belongs to them. Consent should be informed (they know where the video will be shown) and documented for anything beyond classroom use; a refusal must be respected without argument.

questions.stem: Before sharing the exported video, the credits roll too fast to read and one team member's name is misspelled. What does this tell you about process?
choices: Credits do not matter, so ignore it
Always watch the exported file fully before sharing, and hold text on screen long enough to be read aloud twice with spelling checked
Export again at double the frame rate so the credits move faster
Remove the credits entirely to avoid the problem
questions.explanation: The full watch-through of the exported file is the last quality gate — it catches exactly these issues: timing, legibility, spelling, clipped endings. Credits name real people, so errors there are the most embarrassing kind.

questions.stem: A team has five hours to produce a two-minute video about the school garden. Which time split best reflects good practice?
choices: Five minutes planning, four and a half hours filming, no editing time
About an hour on pre-production (script, storyboard, shot list), two hours filming with a planned shot list, two hours editing and reviewing the export
Five hours filming whatever looks interesting, edit nothing
Four hours designing the title card, one hour filming everything
questions.explanation: Quality video balances all three phases: planning makes filming fast and complete, a shot list prevents wasted shooting, and editing plus review is where the film is actually made. Skipping any phase shows in the result.
